samples.text:
The bar chart shows how many people worked in manufacturing, mining and services in a region in 1980 and 2020, and the line graph shows the unemployment rate in the region from 1980 to 2020.

In the bar chart, manufacturing had 310 thousand workers in 1980 but it fell to 120 thousand in 2020. Mining also decreased very much from 95 thousand to only 8 thousand workers. However, services was different, it increased from 240 thousand to 520 thousand workers, so it became the biggest sector.

In the line graph, the unemployment was 5.1% in 1980. Then it rise sharply to 13.8% in 1985, which was the highest. After that it went down gradually to 11.2% in 1990, 9.4% in 1995, 7.6% in 2000 and 6.1% in 2005. In 2010 it increased again to 8.9%, but then it fell to 6.4% in 2015 and 5.3% in 2020.

Overall, the number of people in manufacturing and mining went down but services went up a lot. The unemployment rate went up and down, but in 2020 it was nearly same as 1980.
samples.why: Overview simple and placed at the end · key figures accurate though listed · mechanical linking · repetitive verbs (went up, went down) · errors in verb form, articles and a comma splice.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares the number of people working in three sectors in a region in 1980 and 2020, and the line graph shows how the region's unemployment rate changed over the same forty years.

Overall, employment shifted dramatically from manufacturing and mining to services. Unemployment fluctuated considerably, peaking in the mid-1980s, but by 2020 it had returned almost the same level as in 1980.

In 1980, manufacturing was the largest employer, with 310 thousand workers, followed by services with 240 thousand and mining with 95 thousand. By 2020, however, the number of manufacturing jobs had dropped to 120 thousand, and mining had almost disappeared, employing just 8 thousand people. In contrast, the services sector more than doubled its workforce to 520 thousand.

As for unemployment, the rate was 5.1% in 1980 but soared to 13.8% within five years. It then fell steadily over the next two decades, reaching 6.1% in 2005. There was a further rise to 8.9% in 2010, although this was much smaller than the earlier one, and the rate then decreased again to 6.4% in 2015 and 5.3% in 2020, which was only slightly higher than at the start.
samples.why: Clear overview of the sectoral shift and unemployment pattern · key features well selected · logical paragraphs with good cohesion · some less common vocabulary (soared, workforce) · one minor slip.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares employment in manufacturing, mining and services in a region in 1980 and 2020, while the line graph tracks the regional unemployment rate over the intervening four decades.

The region's economy underwent a profound structural change, with services replacing manufacturing and mining as the main source of jobs. Unemployment was volatile, surging in the early 1980s and rising again around 2010, yet by 2020 it had fallen back almost to its 1980 level.

Manufacturing was the leading employer in 1980, with 310 thousand workers, but by 2020 its workforce had shrunk by more than half to 120 thousand. The contraction in mining was even more severe, from 95 thousand jobs to just 8 thousand. Services moved in the opposite direction, more than doubling from 240 thousand to 520 thousand workers, so that total employment across the three sectors was almost unchanged.

The unemployment rate rose from 5.1% in 1980 to a peak of 13.8% in 1985, before declining steadily to 6.1% by 2005. A second, smaller increase took it to 8.9% in 2010, after which it eased again, standing at 5.3% in 2020, only marginally above the rate forty years earlier.
samples.why: Insightful overview synthesising both visuals · key features selected with accurate comparisons (total employment unchanged) · skilful cohesion · precise vocabulary (structural, contraction, volatile) · wide range of error-free structures.
